1.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, when all these things are come upon thee, the blessing and the curse, which I have set before thee, and thou shalt call them to mind among all the nations, whither the Lord thy God hath driven thee, And shalt return unto the Lord thy God, and shalt obey his voice according to all that I command thee this day, thou and thy children, with all thine heart, and with all thy soul; That then the Lord thy God will turn thy captivity, and have compassion upon thee, and will return and gather thee from all the nations, whither the Lord thy God hath scattered thee. If any of thine be driven out unto the outmost parts of heaven, from thence will the Lord thy God gather thee, and from thence will he fetch thee: And the Lord thy God will bring thee into the land which thy fathers possessed, and thou shalt possess it; and he will do thee good, and multiply thee above thy fathers.

schools.summary: Explain why a blessing is named at all in a survey of coming judgment, since even in the deepest apostasy there would always be a holy seed which could not die out, the nation being otherwise utterly and for ever rejected and the promises of God brought to nothing; then read the gathering soberly, holding that though the Lord would fetch the rejected people even from the end of heaven, the promise neither points directly to a gathering of Israel on its ultimate conversion to Christ nor furnishes any proof that the Jews will then be brought back to Palestine. Note also that since the curse is still upon them the chapter contemplates a restoration still to come, that an awakening among the people must precede it, and that the Hebrew verb for turning the captivity is neuter rather than active — the ground of a rabbinic inference that the Shechinah abides with Israel in captivity and returns with them, though the same form is used of Moab elsewhere.

Confirm that God never so severely afflicts his Church as to be unready to return to mercy, and that punishments cruel in appearance are an invitation to repentance; but limit the offer, since reconciliation is not held out indiscriminately but belongs by peculiar privilege to the Church, and within it only to the residue of the seed, the remnant of grace — for it profits hypocrites mixed among believers no more than strangers to be smitten with the scourges of God. Observe that the phrase from thence is repeated twice, lest the distance of an unknown country be imagined an impediment to what God has promised; and take the dispersion as reaching to the uttermost parts, including these remote islands and, on one learned Jewish opinion, America. Read the promise of return to the land as still future, since many passages say the Jews on their conversion in the latter day will possess Judea again.

Read the passage chiefly as a conditional promise belonging to all persons and all peoples and not to Israel only, whose design is to assure us that the greatest sinners on repentance shall be pardoned and restored to favour, this being the purport of the covenant of grace, which leaves room for repentance as the covenant of innocency did not. Trace the repentance through its stages: it begins in serious consideration, calling to mind what had been forgotten, since consideration is the first step towards conversion and the prodigal came to himself before he came to his father; what is called to mind is the blessing and the curse, as the prodigal weighed his poverty against the plenty of bread in his father's house; and its life and soul is the actual returning to the Lord.

Insist that the promises of this chapter have never yet been fulfilled, since a dispersion among all nations must refer to a wider captivity than the Babylonian and the repossession of the land must therefore be something other than the return from Chaldea; and observe that God so fully foresaw the bad use this people would make of their free agency in resisting the Holy Ghost that he speaks of their sin and punishment as certain, while at the same time showing them how they might turn to him and live even under his indignation.

debates.question: Has the gathering promised here already happened?

sides.position: No: a dispersion among all nations means a wider captivity than the Babylonian, so the repossession must be other than the return from Chaldea
No: a future restoration to Judea at the conversion of the Jews is the plain sense of many passages, some of the dispersed being in these remote islands and, on one Jewish opinion, in America
It is very difficult to read the words of any land but Palestine, and Jeremiah shows their fulfilment in the first restoration — yet the curse still standing means a restoration is still contemplated
The promise neither points directly to a gathering on Israel's ultimate conversion to Christ nor proves that the Jews will then be brought back to Palestine

debates.question: Who are the heavens and earth, or rather who is promised reconciliation?

sides.position: Not all indiscriminately: the blessing belongs to the Church by peculiar privilege and within it only to the remnant of grace
All persons and peoples, since the passage is chiefly a conditional promise that the greatest sinners on repentance shall be pardoned

outliers.note: Alone notices that the Hebrew verb for turning the captivity is neuter rather than active, reports the rabbinic inference that the Shechinah abides with Israel in exile and returns with them, and then undercuts it by observing that the same form is used of Moab in Jeremiah.
Alone locates the dispersion geographically in his own day, in these remote islands once reckoned the uttermost part of the earth and, on Manasseh Ben Israel’s firm belief, in America.

themes: when all these things are come upon thee
the Lord will turn thy captivity

6.pericope_label: And the Lord thy God will circumcise thine heart, and the heart of thy seed, to love the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live. And the Lord thy God will put all these curses upon thine enemies, and on them that hate thee, which persecuted thee. And thou shalt return and obey the voice of the Lord, and do all his commandments which I command thee this day. And the Lord thy God will make thee plenteous in every work of thine hand, in the fruit of thy body, and in the fruit of thy cattle, and in the fruit of thy land, for good: for the Lord will again rejoice over thee for good, as he rejoiced over thy fathers: If thou shalt hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God, to keep his commandments and his statutes which are written in this book of the law, and if thou turn unto the Lord thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul.

schools.summary: Set out what the promise contains — that on true humility God would be found of them, lead them to repentance, sanctify them by the power of his grace, take the stony heart out of their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, a new heart and a new spirit — and cross-refer the language to the prophets who use it. Then settle a point of grammar: the verb rendered thou shalt return is adverbial rather than a second imperative, meaning that Israel would hearken again, and the parallel in the following verse puts this beyond doubt, since the Lord returning and rejoicing plainly means rejoicing again. Read the whole run as the general thought that Israel would then come again into its normal relation to its God and enjoy all the blessings of the covenant.

Call the circumcision of the heart a promise surpassing all the others and refer it to the new covenant, as the prophet interprets it who has God undertake to put his law in their inward parts and write it in their hearts; a divine remedy was needed lest the people fall back into new rebellions, and the chief advantage of their reconciliation is that God should endow them with the Spirit of regeneration. Take the word as alluding to the legal sign of consecration, so that God will create them spiritually new men, cleansed from the filth of flesh and world; and draw the sacramental lesson, that circumcision was the sacrament of repentance as baptism is now, that the letter is useless in itself since many are baptized to no profit, and that whatever God offers in a sacrament depends on the secret operation of his Spirit. Then refuse to let the promise swallow the duty: the perseverance just declared to be God's gift alone is here required of the people, so that they deal foolishly who estimate the powers of man by the commands of God.

Argue from this verse against expecting a national restoration on any other terms, since the heart of that people has never yet been circumcised, the law properly speaking made no provision for a circumcision of the heart, and circumcision itself was only the sign of a spiritual good — so the promise belongs to the days of the Messiah and cannot be fulfilled to the Jews except in their embracing the gospel, which makes it idle to look for their restoration while obstinacy and unbelief remain. Or reach the same place by the order of events, that God will first convert and sanctify them, the fruit of which is that they return and obey, and only then that they prosper. Add the observation that in the threatenings of the previous chapter God is called simply the Lord, a God of power and judge of all, while in these ten verses of promise he is called the Lord thy God twelve times.

debates.question: When is the circumcision of the heart fulfilled?

sides.position: In the new covenant, as Jeremiah interprets it — the Spirit of regeneration given, the man created spiritually new
In the days of the Messiah only, so that it cannot be fulfilled to the Jews except in their embracing the gospel, which makes looking for a restoration idle while unbelief remains
Principally in the times of the gospel, God first converting and sanctifying, with obedience and prosperity following in that order
In the conversion still to come, when the stony heart is taken away and a new spirit given, as the prophets describe
In the conversion of the Jews, described stage by stage — the heart pricked, the hardness removed, the willingness to part with their own righteousness

debates.question: Is the tenth verse a condition or a promise?

sides.position: A renewed enforcement of the indispensable condition of salvation
Not if but for or when, since it has already been promised that God would circumcise their hearts and that they should obey
A warning that they should not receive the grace of God in vain, since grace does not discharge a man's obligation to his duty

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a doctrine of sacraments, that circumcision was the sacrament of repentance as baptism is now, that the letter is useless in itself since many are baptized to no profit, and that all the efficacy of a sacrament is lodged in the secret operation of the Spirit.

Alone counts the divine names, observing that in the threatenings of the previous chapter God is called simply the Lord while in these ten verses of promise he is called the Lord thy God twelve times.

themes: the Lord will again rejoice over thee
the Lord thy God with all thine heart

11.pericope_label: For this commandment which I command thee this day, it is not hidden from thee, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go up for us to heaven, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? Neither is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it? But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it.

schools.summary: Commend the law for its easiness, since God does not propound obscure enigmas to keep our minds in suspense and torment us with difficulties but teaches familiarly whatever is necessary, according to the capacity and therefore the ignorance of the people; nothing is required but diligent application, so that every pretext for ignorance is removed and men cannot err except by wilfully shutting their eyes. From this turn on those who hold scripture to be beset with thick darkness and drive the people away from it as from a labyrinth, since they must either accuse the Holy Spirit of falsehood or malign the book itself; and add that if the ancient people were left without excuse when they had the law for their mistress, our stupidity deserves double and triple condemnation. Note also that the apostle taught us to read the commandment here of the word of faith rather than of the law, which suits the prophecies of conversion just delivered.

Take the commandment for the great command of loving and obeying God, the sum of the law, but not as it stands in itself — rather as softened and accompanied with the grace of the gospel, so that although the practice of God's laws is far from us and above our strength, with that grace it is near and easy to those who believe, which is how the verse agrees with the apostle's use of it for the righteousness of faith. Keep the two impossibilities concrete, that the knowledge was not to be fetched from far distant places to which the wise heathen travelled for their wisdom but was brought to their very doors and declared to them in the wilderness; assign the mouth to the promises forming part of every Jew's creed and the heart to the power of believing unto righteousness; and conclude that the law is plain and easy but the gospel much more so.

Take this commandment, as the phrase is used earlier in the book, to denote the whole law, and state the two denials flatly: it is not too wonderful, that is, not too hard to grasp or unintelligible, and not too far off — neither in heaven at an inaccessible height nor beyond the sea at an unattainable distance at the end of the world, so that no one could ask who is able to fetch it thence. Observe that the law not only lay before the people in writing but was preached to them by word of mouth and so brought within their knowledge; and note that the fulfilment of the condition just stated is therefore neither impossible nor really very difficult, God having done everything to render obedience possible.

Urge obedience from the plainness and easiness of the command, since they could never plead that God had enjoined what was unintelligible or impracticable. No messengers need be sent to heaven to enquire what will please God, nor any voyage made overseas as the philosophers made who travelled through many and distant regions in pursuit of learning; the commandment is not reserved to those of great estate or refined genius. It is written in their books and made plain upon tables so that he who runs may read; it is not communicated in a strange language but in the vulgar tongue commonly used, so that it may be heard read and talked of familiarly among the children; and it is not wrapped in obscure phrases or hieroglyphics but delivered so as to be level to the meanest capacity.

sides.position: The word of faith, the gospel preached, as the apostle taught us to read it
The doctrine of salvation to be proclaimed in their own land, since the Saviour is to be born at Bethlehem and the prophet raised up from among their brethren
The whole law, as the phrase is used earlier in the book
The great command of loving and obeying God, not as it stands in itself but as softened and accompanied with the grace of the gospel

debates.question: In what sense is it not far off?

sides.position: No messengers need be sent to heaven, and no voyage made overseas as the philosophers made in pursuit of learning
It is neither at an inaccessible height nor at an unattainable distance at the end of the world
Salvation is of the Jews, so they need not travel to distant nations for it
God does not propound obscure enigmas but teaches familiarly according to the capacity of the people, so that no pretext for ignorance remains

outliers.note: Alone turns the easiness of the law into a polemic on the clarity of scripture, against those who hold it beset with thick darkness and drive the people away from it as from a labyrinth.

Alone spells out the two excuses the verse forecloses, sending messengers to heaven and voyaging overseas as the philosophers did, and adds that the commandment is not reserved to men of estate or refined genius.

themes: it is not hidden from thee
who shall go up for us to heaven
the word is very nigh unto thee

15.pericope_label: See, I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil; In that I command thee this day to love the Lord thy God, to walk in his ways, and to keep his commandments and his statutes and his judgments, that thou mayest live and multiply: and the Lord thy God shall bless thee in the land whither thou goest to possess it. But if thine heart turn away, so that thou wilt not hear, but shalt be drawn away, and worship other gods, and serve them; I denounce unto you this day, that ye shall surely perish, and that ye shall not prolong your days upon the land, whither thou passest over Jordan to go to possess it.

schools.summary: Read the setting of life and death before them as depriving Israel of any pretext of error, since they are separated from the heathen nations which through ignorance of the right way vacillated as in uncertainty between the two; and reproach them as more than senseless if, when no one under the guidance of nature would fail to seek life and recoil from death, they should plunge voluntarily into all miseries. Insist that these are not idle menaces but doctrine armed with the power of God, so that whoever embraces it finds salvation and none despises it with impunity; and call the promises and threats the sanctions of the law, since its authority is assured to us only when both the recompense of obedience and the punishment of transgression are set before us. Take the clause about being drawn away not as excusing their instability but as aggravating the crime, since they are carried off as by a whirlpool by their own depraved desires and desert a truth they knew well.

Admire the construction of the appeal, so rational, so prudent and so affectionate that it shows the speaker in earnest and leaves the hearers inexcusable, and show that it works on the two springs of human action. Every man covets to obtain life and good and to escape death and evil, and the way to obtain all the happiness he can desire has been shown him; every man is moved and governed by hope and fear, and both have now been tried, so that whoever will be wrought on either way is kept close to his duty and whoever will not is utterly without excuse. Add the reflection on knowledge: our first parents ate the forbidden fruit hoping to gain the knowledge of good and evil and got a miserable knowledge, of good by the loss of it and of evil by the sense of it, whereas God has since favoured man by his word with such a knowledge of both as will make him happy for ever if it be not his own fault.

Ask why life and death were set before them at all, and answer in four steps: that they might comprehend their import, that they might feel their importance, that they might choose the path of believing and loving obedience, and that so choosing they and their posterity might be God's favourites in time and eternity. Then press the argument these steps imply, that were there no such thing as free will in man nobody could reconcile such sayings with either sincerity or common sense; hold that God made the human will free in creation and formed the soul accordingly, that no power in heaven, earth or hell save God's own can deprive it of its free volitions, and that law and gospel, promise and precept, the denunciation of woe and the doctrine of eternal life are all constructed on that ground. Derive accountability from it, since a man's actions are his and therefore rewardable and punishable, whereas actions necessitated by fate would not be his; and add that liberty is implied in the very idea of volition.

debates.question: What does the setting of life and death before them prove?

sides.position: The freedom of the will, without which the sayings could not be reconciled with sincerity or common sense, and from which accountability follows
That Israel has no pretext of error, being separated from nations that vacillated through ignorance, and is more than senseless if it plunges voluntarily into misery
That every man is moved by hope and fear, both of which have now been tried, so that whoever will not be wrought on either way is inexcusable

debates.question: Does being drawn away lessen the guilt?

sides.position: No — it is named to aggravate the crime, since they are carried off by their own depraved desires and desert a truth they knew well
The turning away is from the true God and from his commands, statutes and judgments

outliers.note: Alone builds a full argument for the freedom of the will out of the verse, holding that law and gospel alike are constructed on that ground and that liberty is implied in the very idea of volition.

Alone contrasts the knowledge of good and evil got by eating the forbidden fruit — of good by the loss of it and of evil by the sense of it — with the knowledge of both that God has since given by his word.

themes: life and good, death and evil

19.pericope_label: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live: That thou mayest love the Lord thy God, and that thou mayest obey his voice, and that thou mayest cleave unto him: for he is thy life, and the length of thy days: that thou mayest dwell in the land which the Lord sware unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.

schools.summary: Settle the syntax of the exhortation, taking the words about choosing as the apodosis of the sentence, so that the calling of heaven and earth to witness is what the command to choose life depends on; and gloss the closing clause exactly, that the Lord being thy life means the loving of him is the condition of life and of long life in the promised land. Hear in the same clause the Old Testament form of the well-known saying about the resurrection and the life, which may yet be fulfilled in Israel.

Deny that the summoning of heaven and earth addresses men and angels, as some tamely expound it, holding rather that sense is attributed to things inanimate by way of amplification, and note that the past-tense verb indicates a present act, the witnesses being called to deal with the hearers more urgently. Then meet the difficulty in the command to choose. As respects its doctrine the law contains life and death, since the reward of eternal life is not promised in it in vain; but because no one is found worthy the apostle justly teaches that the law ministers death, which is accidental and proceeds from the corruption of men, not from any fault in the doctrine. How then can a life the sinner cannot reach by the law be commanded him? Opponents lift their crests here to extol free will and boast of merits; the answer is that Moses also proclaims the gratuitous mercy of God and directs his disciples to Christ, so that keeping the commandments does not exclude the twofold grace by which the regenerate aspire to obedience while being freely pardoned — and since the same covenant is common to us and the ancient people, those who of old embraced this doctrine did choose life.

Take the three verbs of the last verse as a chain in which no link holds alone: without love there can be no obedience, without obedience love is fruitless and dead, and without close attachment and perseverance a temporary love however sincere and fervent will be ultimately ineffectual, since he alone who endures to the end shall be saved. Turn on a particular confidence, that those who talk most strenuously about the impossibility of falling from grace are commonly those who have not yet tasted that the Lord is gracious, and ask how absurd it is to dispute about arriving safely at the end of a way in which a man has never taken one hearty step. Then expound the clause that God is their life by accumulation, since he gives life, preserves it, restores it and prolongs it by his power though it be frail and by his presence though it be forfeited, sweetens it by his comforts and completes all in life everlasting; and state the bare consequence, that they shall have life who choose it and that those who come short must thank themselves, since they die because they will die.

debates.question: Who or what is called to witness?

sides.position: Things inanimate, sense being attributed to them by amplification — not men and angels, as some tamely expound it
Either the heavens and earth literally, as inanimate bodies often called as witnesses, or figuratively their inhabitants, angels and men

debates.question: How can a sinner be commanded to choose a life the law cannot give him?

sides.position: Because Moses also proclaims gratuitous mercy and directs his disciples to Christ; keeping the commandments does not exclude the twofold grace of regeneration and free pardon
Because those shall have life who choose it, and those who come short must thank themselves, dying because they will die
Because loving the Lord is itself the condition of life and of long life in the land
Nothing but perseverance itself: without love no obedience, without obedience love is dead, and without attachment a temporary love is ultimately ineffectual
God himself, who gives, preserves, restores and prolongs life by his power and presence, and completes all in life everlasting

outliers.note: Alone states the difficulty in the command to choose life as an objection against himself, granting that the law ministers death and that opponents lift their crests at this point, before answering from the twofold grace.

Alone turns on those who talk strenuously about the impossibility of falling from grace, asking how absurd it is to dispute about arriving safely at the end of a way in which a man has never taken one hearty step.

themes: I call heaven and earth to record
he is thy life, and the length of thy days
